Fulsome

FUL-sum · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fulsome is expressing praise or flattery to an excessive, insincere degree.

The obituary's fulsome tribute struck several old colleagues as more strategic than sincere.

Worked Example

The critic's fulsome praise for the mediocre film made readers wonder if he'd been paid to write it.

Praise so over-the-top for a mediocre film that readers suspect a bribe is exactly fulsome.

How Fulsome Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

gushing

gushing: expressing enthusiasm in an excessive, insincere way

effusive

effusive: expressing feelings in an unrestrained, excessive manner

Antonyms

understated

understated: expressed with restraint, less than fully

How Strong Is It? — generous → fulsome → obsequious

generous vs. fulsome

generous vs. fulsome: Generous praise is warm and kind, often perfectly sincere; fulsome specifically implies the praise has gone too far to feel genuine.

obsequious vs. fulsome

obsequious vs. fulsome: Obsequious (taught earlier in this course) describes an overall eager-to-please manner toward a person, while fulsome specifically describes the excessive quality of praise or language itself.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — ful

root — ful: full, complete (Old English)

suffix — -some

suffix — -some: characterized by, tending to (Old English)

Put it together

Put it together: Fulsome is a native English formation: full + -some -- literally 'full of' something, which over time narrowed to mean 'excessively, insincerely full' of praise.

Use the root in a new word: wholesome

Use the root in a new word: wholesome: The same -some suffix appears in the everyday word wholesome ('characterized by health and wellbeing'), built the same way on a different base word.

Root Check

Word Choice

Fulsome describes praise, apology, or language so excessive that it starts to feel insincere or self-serving -- it is almost never a compliment to call something fulsome.
